passages.t: God has spoken in his Son
passages.happening:
The letter has no greeting. It begins straight away with God.

“On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe” (verses 1-2).

Then the writer says who this Son is. “The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature, upholding all things by His powerful word” (verse 3). He tells what the Son has done: “After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (verse 3). And he ends with a comparison that the rest of the chapter will explain: “So He became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
In Greek these four verses are one long sentence, carefully shaped, with a rhythm that sounds well when read aloud. The letter was meant to be heard.

The first readers knew that God had spoken to Israel's fathers. He spoke to Abraham, to Moses, to Samuel, to Isaiah and Jeremiah, in visions and dreams, in laws and songs and stories. Every word was true. But each was a part. Now, the writer says, God has spoken his last and fullest word, and that word is a person, his Son. ‘These last days’ means the time that began when the Son came.

Look at what is said of the Son. He is the heir: everything will be his. He is the one through whom God made the universe. He is ‘the radiance of God’s glory’: as the brightness of the sun is the sun's own light shining out, so the Son is God's own glory shining. He is ‘the exact representation of His nature’. The Greek word was used for the mark a stamp leaves in wax, or the image struck on a coin. To see the Son is to see what God is like. And he holds the whole world together by his word.

Then comes a surprise in the middle of all this glory: ‘purification for sins’. That is the language of priests and sacrifices, of washing away what makes people unclean before God. The rest of the letter will explain how the Son did it, by offering himself. When it was done, he ‘sat down’. The letter will say later that the priests stood day after day to do their work, because it was never finished (10:11). The Son sat, because his was.

Angels were the highest beings people could imagine below God. Many Jews of the time believed that angels had helped give the law at Sinai (2:2; see also Acts 7:53). To show that the Son is higher than the angels is to show that his message outranks even the law given through them.
passages.ot:
The opening line looks back over the whole Old Testament. God did speak through prophets: “Surely the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7). And he spoke ‘in many different ways’. To most prophets he spoke in visions and dreams, but to Moses “face to face, clearly and not in riddles” (Numbers 12:8).

‘Heir of all things’ recalls the promise God makes to his king in Psalm 2: “Ask Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance, the ends of the earth Your possession” (Psalm 2:8). In its own setting this was a promise to the king of David's line in Jerusalem. Hebrews hears it fulfilled in the Son.

‘Through whom He made the universe’: the psalms say God made the world by his word, “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made” (Psalm 33:6). Proverbs pictures God's wisdom beside him at creation: “I was there when He established the heavens” (Proverbs 8:27). In Proverbs, wisdom speaks like a person, as a picture of God's wisdom. Hebrews says something those writers did not say: the one through whom God made all things is a person, the Son, and that Son also made purification for sins.

‘Purification for sins’ echoes the Day of Atonement, the most solemn day of Israel's year: “on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD” (Leviticus 16:30).

And ‘sat down at the right hand’ comes from the psalm Hebrews will quote at the end of the chapter: “The LORD said to my Lord: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet’” (Psalm 110:1).
passages.hard:
If the Son made the universe, how can he be ‘appointed heir’, and how can he ‘become’ superior to the angels? Was he once less than God?

No. The letter says the Son was there before the world, for God made the universe through him (verse 2). He was not made. Yet the same Son became a man. As a man he was ‘made a little lower than the angels’ for a while, and suffered and died (2:9). Then God raised him and seated him at his right hand. ‘Became superior’ and ‘appointed heir’ describe that path: the eternal Son, having taken our nature and finished his work, was enthroned as the Messiah over all things, in the nature he took for us. Nothing was added to him as God. What changed is that a man now sits on the throne of heaven.

The church confesses what these verses say. The Nicene Creed confesses Jesus Christ as ‘God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father, by whom all things were made’. ‘Light of Light’ comes close to verse 3: the Son is the light that shines from the light. And the same creed says that he ‘came down from heaven’ and ‘was made man’. The Council of Chalcedon in AD 451 confessed him as one person, ‘truly God and truly man’. These are not the site's own views. They are the faith of the church, and these verses are one of the places that faith comes from.

So this opening sentence holds both truths together. The Son shares the very nature of God. And the Son came into our history, at a certain time, to deal with our sins. The next chapter will say how fully human he became.
passages.asks: God has spoken, and his clearest word is a person. Ask whether you listen for God mainly in rules and ideas, or in the Son himself. Ask what it means that the one who holds the world together also stooped to wash away your sins. And ask what it means that he sat down: is there a way in which you are still trying to finish a work for God that Christ has already finished?

passages.t: ‘You are My Son’: the angels worship him
passages.happening:
Now the writer begins to show from Scripture that the Son is above the angels. He asks a question: “For to which of the angels did God ever say: ‘You are My Son; today I have become Your Father’? Or again: ‘I will be His Father, and He will be My Son’?” (verse 5).

The answer is that God never said such words to any angel. He said them to his king.

Then a second step. “And again, when God brings His firstborn into the world, He says: ‘Let all God’s angels worship Him’” (verse 6). The angels do not stand beside the Son as equals. They bow before him.
passages.hearers:
From here to the end of the chapter, the writer strings together seven passages from the Old Testament, mostly from the psalms. He brings them in as words God says, not only as words written long ago. The first readers knew these passages well, and they would have followed each step.

The chain begins and ends with the same question: ‘to which of the angels did God ever say’ (verses 5 and 13). It is like the two ends of a bridge.

‘Son of God’ was a title for Israel's king. When a king of David's line was crowned, God took him as his son, to rule for him. Angels could be called ‘sons of God’ as a group in the Old Testament (Job 1:6), but no single angel was ever told, ‘You are My Son’. That word was spoken to the king, and the king pointed ahead to the Messiah.

‘Firstborn’ in the Bible means more than the child born first. It means the one with the highest rank, who receives the inheritance. It does not mean the Son was created. The same chapter calls him the maker of earth and heaven (verse 10).

Many Jews of the time gave angels great honour. Some Christians were tempted to give them too much (Colossians 2:18). Hebrews says plainly that the angels worship the Son. So he is not one of them.
passages.ot:
Verse 5 joins two promises to David's line. The first is Psalm 2. It is a royal psalm, a psalm about Israel's king. Many scholars think it was first sung when a new king of David's line was crowned in Jerusalem, as the site's note on that psalm says. God's word over the king is, “I will proclaim the decree spoken to Me by the LORD: ‘You are My Son; today I have become Your Father’” (Psalm 2:7). The ‘today’ was the day the king took his throne.

The second is God's promise to David through the prophet Nathan, about the son who would follow him: “I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom” (2 Samuel 7:12). “I will be his Father, and he will be My son” (2 Samuel 7:14). In its first setting it pointed to Solomon, David's son who built the temple. The same verse goes on, “When he does wrong, I will discipline him”, because the kings of David's line were human and sinful. But the promise of a throne ‘forever’ (2 Samuel 7:13) was bigger than any of them. Israel came to hope for a son of David who would fulfil it, and Hebrews says Jesus is that son.

Verse 6 quotes a line from the end of the Song of Moses: “Rejoice, O heavens, with Him, and let all God’s angels worship Him” (Deuteronomy 32:43). That line is found in the longer form of the verse kept in the Greek Old Testament and in a copy found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the Berean Standard Bible follows that longer form. In the Song it is a call for heaven to praise the LORD, who saves his people. Psalm 97 has a similar call: “Worship Him, all you gods!” (Psalm 97:7). Hebrews applies the words to the Son, which it could only do if the Son is the LORD to whom the worship belongs.

‘Firstborn’ recalls God's promise about David's heir: “I will indeed appoint him as My firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth” (Psalm 89:27).
passages.hard:
‘Today I have become Your Father.’ Does this mean the Son began to exist on some day, or became God's Son only at a certain time?

No. In Psalm 2 the ‘today’ was a coronation day: the king did not begin to live that day; he began to reign. The New Testament hears the same word spoken over Jesus at the great turning points of his work. Paul, preaching in Antioch, said God had kept his promise “by raising up Jesus. As it is written in the second Psalm: ‘You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.’” (Acts 13:33). For Paul, the ‘today’ was Easter, when the Son who had always been the Son was raised and enthroned in power.

The church confesses that the Son is eternal. The Nicene Creed says he was ‘begotten of his Father before all worlds’ and ‘begotten, not made’. ‘Begotten’ there does not mean he had a beginning. It means he shares the Father's own nature, as a son shares his father's nature, and has done so always. Hebrews itself has already said that God made the universe through him (verse 2).

Why does ‘when God brings His firstborn into the world’ (verse 6) not say when? Readers differ. Some think of his birth, when angels praised God over Bethlehem (Luke 2:13-14). Some think of his rising and return to heaven, when he entered the ‘world to come’ (2:5). Some think of his return in glory. The point is the same on every reading: wherever the Son is brought, the angels worship him.
passages.asks: The angels, the highest of creatures, bow before the Son. Ask where your own worship goes, and whether anything has taken the place that belongs to him. And ask what it means to be loved by a God who calls his king ‘Son’, and who, as the letter will say, is not ashamed to call us his brothers and sisters (2:11).

passages.happening:
Now the writer sets the angels and the Son side by side.

“Now about the angels He says: ‘He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire’” (verse 7).

“But about the Son He says: ‘Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, Your God, has anointed You above Your companions with the oil of joy’” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
The contrast is strong. The angels are like wind and fire: powerful, quick, sent here and there to do God's work. They are servants. The Son is spoken to as a king on a throne that lasts forever.

A sceptre was the rod a king held as the sign of his rule. This king's sceptre is ‘justice’. He loves what is right and hates what is evil.

To ‘anoint’ was to pour oil on someone's head to set them apart. Kings were anointed in Israel. The Hebrew word for ‘anointed one’ gives us ‘Messiah’, and the Greek word gives us ‘Christ’. The ‘oil of joy’ was the oil of a festival, a sign of gladness. This king is anointed above his ‘companions’, the other kings, or all who share in his kingdom.

Notice the two names in verses 8 and 9. The Son is called ‘God’: ‘Your throne, O God’. And yet ‘God, Your God, has anointed You’. The Son is God, and he is not the Father. In a small space, Christians have seen here what the church later named the Trinity.
passages.ot:
Verse 7 quotes Psalm 104, a great song of praise for God's care of creation. In the Berean Standard Bible the line reads, “He makes the winds His messengers, flames of fire His servants” (Psalm 104:4). The psalm is about the weather: God uses the winds and the lightning as his servants. The Hebrew word for ‘messengers’ is also the word for ‘angels’, and the word for ‘winds’ also means ‘spirits’. So the line can be read more than one way. Hebrews follows the Greek Old Testament, which reads it as God making his angels like winds and flames. The point holds either way: angels, like wind and fire, are creatures God sends.

Verses 8 and 9 quote Psalm 45, a song for a royal wedding. In its own setting it praised a king of David's line on his wedding day. “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you above your companions with the oil of joy” (Psalm 45:6-7).

The prophet Isaiah also spoke of a royal child: “And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6).
passages.hard:
Psalm 45 was sung for a king of Israel. Is a human king really called ‘God’, and how can Hebrews read the line of Jesus?

It is honest to say that translators differ about the psalm, as the site's note on Psalm 45 says. The Hebrew most naturally reads ‘Your throne, O God’, as words spoken to the king, and most English Bibles print it that way. Some scholars think this was court language: the king stood for God, and the Hebrew word for God is sometimes used of human rulers or judges. Other translations avoid calling the king God, with readings such as ‘your divine throne’. Jewish readers have read the line in more than one way, as words to the king or as words to God himself.

Hebrews does not claim that the first singers had Jesus in mind. It reads the psalm as part of one story that has now reached its goal. If Jesus is the promised Son of David, the royal psalms find their true king in him. And if the Son is the one through whom God made the universe (verse 2), then words that call the king ‘God’ fit him fully, not as a courtly title, but as the truth. Many Christians grant that the first singer may have meant something smaller, which later history filled out.

What Christians confess here is what the creeds confess: the Son is ‘very God of very God’, of one being with the Father, and yet he is not the Father. ‘Your throne, O God’ and ‘God, Your God, has anointed You’ stand side by side in these verses, and the church has never let go of either.
passages.asks: The angels are wind and fire, sent to serve. The Son is king, and his sceptre is justice. Ask whether you trust that the one who rules the world loves what is right and hates what is evil. Ask where you need that today, in the face of a wrong done to you or by you. And ask whether his joy, the ‘oil of joy’, has any place in the way you follow him.

passages.t: The unchanging maker, seated at God's right hand
passages.happening:
The writer quotes one more psalm about the Son, and it is the most startling yet.

“In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands. They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment. You will roll them up like a robe; like a garment they will be changed; but You remain the same, and Your years will never end” (verses 10-12).

Then the chain ends where it began, with a question. “Yet to which of the angels did God ever say: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet’?” (verse 13).

And the answer about the angels: “Are not the angels ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation?” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
To the first readers, the world must have seemed the most lasting thing there was: the ground under their feet, the sky over their heads. The psalm says even these will wear out, like an old coat that is folded up and put away. Only God does not wear out. Hebrews says this of the Son. Everything else changes. He stays the same. The letter will say it again near the end: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (13:8).

For readers who had lost property and friends, and who were tired, this mattered. What they could see was shaking. The one they trusted was not.

To sit at a king's right hand was to hold the place of highest honour and share his rule. A footstool under the feet was a picture of complete victory. God never offered that seat to an angel.

And then a gentle turn. The angels are ‘sent to serve’. Whom do they serve? Not only God, but ‘those who will inherit salvation’, God's people. The mighty beings of wind and fire are sent out for the sake of ordinary believers.
passages.ot:
Verses 10 to 12 come from Psalm 102. That psalm is “A prayer of one who is afflicted, when he grows faint and pours out his lament before the LORD” (Psalm 102:1). A sick and lonely man feels his days passing like smoke. Then he turns to the God who does not pass away: “In the beginning You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands. They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment. Like clothing You will change them, and they will be passed on. But You remain the same, and Your years will never end” (Psalm 102:25-27).

In the psalm these words are spoken to the LORD, Israel's God. The wording in Hebrews differs a little, with ‘O Lord’ in the first line and ‘You will roll them up like a robe’, because the writer usually follows the Greek Old Testament. And Hebrews reads the words as spoken to the Son. That is a high claim: the words for the Creator belong to him.

Verse 13 quotes Psalm 110, a psalm of David: “The LORD said to my Lord: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet’” (Psalm 110:1). In its own setting it is God's word to a king, as the site's note on Psalm 110 explains. It is the Old Testament verse most often quoted or echoed in the New Testament, and Jesus himself asked how David could call his own descendant ‘Lord’ (Matthew 22:42-45).

The Old Testament also shows angels sent to guard God's people: “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them” (Psalm 34:7).
passages.hard:
Psalm 102 is a prayer to the LORD. How can Hebrews take words spoken to God the Creator and apply them to Jesus?

Hebrews does not say that the man who prayed Psalm 102 was thinking of Jesus. It reads the psalm in the light of what it has already said in verse 2: God made the universe through the Son. If that is true, then the praise of the Creator rightly belongs to the Son as well. The early church did the same elsewhere. Paul takes words from Isaiah about the LORD, that every knee will bow to him, and applies them to Jesus (Philippians 2:10-11). John says of the Word, “Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made” (John 1:3).

Readers who find this way of reading the Old Testament strange often find it less so once they see the writer's starting point. He is not proving that the Son is God from scratch. He believes it, with the whole early church, and he shows how the Scriptures sound when that is true.

What of the angels? The Bible says they are real, that they serve God, and that they are sent to help his people (verse 14). It says little more about how they do it. Many Christians take comfort in this verse. It gives no reason to pray to angels or to seek them; in this very chapter they worship the Son, and Colossians warns against the worship of angels (Colossians 2:18). The doctrine study ‘Angels, Satan, and Spiritual Powers’ says more.
passages.asks: Everything you can see will wear out, and Christ will not. Ask what you are leaning on that is passing away. Ask what it would mean to trust the one who ‘remains the same’ in the place where your life is changing. And remember the last verse: God sends even his angels to serve people like you.
